title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Pet grooming
audience: Groomers who set prices or plan monthly income, including those who work from a salon, a home studio or a mobile van.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a home-service business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means for a groomer
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of grooming income that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below it the business loses money; above it, each extra dollar adds to profit. For a groomer, the figure shows how many grooms a month are needed before income adds to profit. It is a planning tool, and its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages that go into it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of grooms. They include rent or a salon share, van registration and repayments, insurance, phone and booking software, equipment servicing contracts, and any registration fee spread over a year. Variable costs move with each groom. They include shampoos and conditioners, blades and blade oil, towels and disposables, fuel for a mobile visit, and any card or booking fee charged on each sale. ANZ defines fixed and variable costs and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss (ANZ, 21 February 2025). Express variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. The quantity one minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin: the share of each dollar of sales left to cover fixed costs. Xero's glossary sets out the same method and says a job count is rounded up to whole jobs (Xero Australia, 23 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Use the price the owner pays
instruction.body: Divide break-even revenue by the average price the owner pays for a groom, on the same price basis as the variable percentage. Vendor price guides show what the market lists, for example a medium full clip at $85 to $100 (Airtasker, 17 March 2025). Your own average sale price, after any discount, is the figure to use in the calculation.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost. Confirm that the output is revenue and not profit. Then write down the reconciled figure with its inputs, and drop the others. A figure that cannot be checked should not be used to set a price.

procedure: List every monthly cost and label it fixed or variable, including any card or booking fee.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average sale price per groom, and round up to whole grooms.
Recalculate when a fixed cost, a card fee or the mix of services changes.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market data. A salon groomer has fixed costs of $2,000 a month (illustrative), variable costs of 12 per cent of sales for shampoo, blades, towels and card fees (illustrative), and an average sale of $90 a groom (illustrative). Airtasker's vendor range for a medium full clip is $85 to $100 (17 March 2025).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many grooms must she complete each month to break even, and what should she check before she sets prices?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.12, which is 0.88. Break-even revenue is $2,000 divided by 0.88, which is $2,272.73 a month. At $90 a groom, that is 25.25 grooms, so she needs 26 grooms a month to cover her costs. Each groom contributes $79.20 towards fixed costs. Before setting prices, she checks that the 12 per cent includes card fees and every consumable, that the $2,000 is a monthly figure, and that $90 is her average sale after any discount.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months, labelled fixed or variable
Sales and card statements for the same months

commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Using a listing price instead of your own average sale
commonErrors.prevention: Use the average sale your own grooms achieve, after discounts.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from another plan
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate from your own records, and record the source and date of each input.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check the tax treatment of costs with a registered tax agent or qualified accountant.
This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority to run a grooming business or a mobile grooming service.
Grooming premises and mobile rules differ by state and territory, and Victorian rules are UNRESOLVED in this research. Use the rule that applies to the place you work when you set fixed costs.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and price basis.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period and one price basis throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs, and do not copy a listing price or another groomer's break-even.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue for a groomer is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $2,000 a month and variable costs are 12% of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same grooming business. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller one
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the owner today
Use the listing prices alone and skip the check
